sources.title: NGSS MS-ESS1-1: Develop and use a model of the Earth-sun-moon system to describe the cyclic patterns of lunar phases, eclipses of the sun and moon, and seasons
OpenStax Astronomy 2e, 4.5 Phases and Motions of the Moon

legend.name: Sunlit half
legend.meaning: The half of the moon facing the sun

legend.name: Dark half
legend.meaning: The half facing away from the sun

legend.name: Earth
legend.meaning: Our planet, seen from far above the North Pole

steps.title: Sunlight
steps.instruction: Draw the three arrows of sunlight coming from the right.

note.text: The sun is far off to the right. Its light comes from about the same direction all month.
We're looking down from far above Earth's North Pole.

steps.title: Moon's orbit
steps.instruction: Trace the moon's path around Earth, with its arrows.

note.text: The moon orbits Earth counterclockwise, seen from above. Its phases repeat about every 29.5 days.
note.remember: One cycle of phases: about 29.5 days.

steps.title: Sunlit halves
steps.instruction: Trace the half of each moon that faces the sun.

note.text: The moon makes no light of its own. It shines by reflected sunlight, and the sun always lights half of it.
note.remember: Half the moon is always lit.

steps.title: Dark halves
steps.instruction: Trace the half of each moon facing away from the sun.

note.text: The phase we see depends on how much of the sunlit half faces Earth.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: Color the sunlit halves, the dark halves and Earth.

steps.title: Name the phases
steps.instruction: Imagine standing on Earth facing each moon. Which phase do you see?

mistakes.Full moon: Its lit half faces the sun, away from us. We see the dark side, so it's a new moon.

targets.role: A quarter of the way around.

mistakes.Third quarter: This is the first quarter: the moon is one quarter of the way around after new moon.

mistakes.New moon: Here the lit half faces Earth too, so we see the whole bright face: a full moon.

targets.role: Three quarters of the way around.

mistakes.First quarter: This is three quarters of the way around after new moon: the third quarter.

steps.title: The cycle
steps.instruction: Tap the phases in order, starting from new moon.
steps.why: After new moon, we see more of the sunlit half each night (waxing) until full moon, then less (waning).
steps.hint: Waxing means growing. It comes before full moon.

steps.title: What causes phases?
steps.question: What causes the phases of the moon?

options.text: We see different amounts of the moon's sunlit half as it orbits Earth
options.feedback: Yes. The sun always lights half the moon. Where the moon is in its orbit decides how much of that half we see.

options.text: Earth's shadow covers part of the moon
options.feedback: A common idea, but no. Earth's shadow only reaches the moon in a lunar eclipse.

options.text: Clouds cover part of the moon
options.feedback: Clouds are in our air, not on the moon. Phases come from the moon's position in its orbit.

options.text: The moon makes less light some nights
options.feedback: The moon makes no light at all. It reflects sunlight, and half of it is always lit.

steps.title: Predict
steps.instruction: Think about where the full moon is.
steps.question: A full moon is opposite the sun in the sky. When does it rise?

options.feedback: Right. Opposite the sun, it rises as the sun sets and stays up all night, setting at sunrise.
That's the new moon, which sits in the same direction as the sun.
The first quarter moon rises around noon. The full moon rises at sunset.
The third quarter moon rises around midnight. The full moon rises at sunset.
